16 IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON MEDICAL IMAGING, VOL. 45, NO. 1, JANUARY 2026
REDNet: Reliable Evidential Discounting
Network for Multi-Modality Medical
Image Segmentation
Shichen Sun
 , Member, IEEE, Yufei Chen
 , Xiaodong Yue
 , Chao Ma, and Xiahai Zhuang
Abstract— In the field of computer-aided diagnosis, par-
ticularly for tumor diseases, segmentation is a prerequisite
and primary step. Multi-modality images become essential
for achieving accurate segmentation, which offer critical
insights beyond the limitations of single-modality data.
However, different modalities and images may suffer from
different types of data imperfection, such as intensity
non-uniformity, motion artifact, and low quality due to
hardware limitations, which challenge image segmentation
algorithms. To address this challenge, we propose a Reli-
able Evidential Discounting Network (REDNet), which is
composed of three main modules: 1) the Intra-modality
Consistency Evaluation Module (ICEM) measuring the data
cohesion within the same modality; 2) the Cross-modality
Difference Aggregation Module (CDAM) identifing data dis-
crepancy across modalities; 3) the Discounting Fusion
Module (DFM) processing the multi-modality evidence by
applying discounting strategies to fuse the data. This
approach maintains segmentation accuracy by effectively
integrating multi-modality evidence, while discounting the
influence of lower-quality data, ensuring reliable results
despite the presence of image imperfections. We evalu-
ated REDNet on two distinct datasets, BRATS2021 and an
in-house pancreas dataset from Changhai Hospital. REDNet
outperforms other methods, particularly in scenarios with
imperfect image sources, and achieves reliable results in
multi-modality tumor segmentation.
Index Terms — Reliable segmentation, multi-modality
data, evidential learning, uncertainty.
I. I NTRODUCTION
M

and accurately delineate organs and tumors, serving as
an essential component for computer-aided diagnosis [1], [2],

[3], [4]. Single-modality medical images often lack the detail
needed for reliable diagnoses, especially for tumors which
prompting researchers to rely on multi-modality imaging to
achieve enhanced segmentation accuracy. Researchers have
designed different networks to improve segmentation perfor-
mance on multi-modality [5], [6], [7].
The performance of existing multi-modal medical image
segmentation frameworks is heavily dependent on high-quality
data from various modalities. In clinic scenarios, images often
suffer from various types of imperfection due to uneven illu-
mination, patient movement, hardware limitations, and other
unexpected factors [8], [9], [10]. Models often perform poorly
when faced with imperfection in one or more modalities.
Furthermore, many researchers have proposed uncertainty
approaches to reduce the impact of imperfection on medi-
cal image segmentation models. Methods such as shadowed
sets [11], ensemble [12] and subjective logic [13] have
shown potently of tackling imperfection. However, Karimi
and Gholipour [14] shows that uncertainty methods are less
effective when there is a substantial discrepancy between test
and training data, which challenges the generalizability. Many
existing models may fail to detect imperfection in the data and
cannot dynamically adjust based on data quality to reduce the
effects of flawed data.
In this work, we propose a reliable evidential discount-
ing network, named REDNet, which not only dynamically
adjusts the contribution of modalities based on their real-time
quality for better segmentation but also actively reduces
the impact of imperfection in multi-modality. REDNet is
composed of three main modules. The Intra-modality Con-
sistency Evaluation Module (ICEM) refines features within
modalities by contrasting test against training data, while
the Cross-modality Difference Aggregation Module (CDAM)
extracts cross-modality insights by observing data discrepancy
across modalities. Unlike previous methods which apply static
weights, the Discounting Fusion Module (DFM) offers an
innovative approach that varies the level of discounting in
response to the observed imperfection in each modality and
fuse the data from different modalities, thereby ensuring
reliable segmentation under diverse conditions.
We conduct experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of the
proposed REDNet on the BRATS2021 challenge dataset [15]
and in-house pancreas dataset. Our model performs well

against both conventional methods and uncertainty-based
methods. Our model demonstrates strong performance in
introducing the impact of imperfection to the data as well
as handling the inherent imperfections present in medical
imaging data. The main contributions of this study are as
follows:
• We propose a reliable evidential discounting network
(REDNet). This framework is designed to dynamically
calibrate the influence of each modality by assessing their
real-time quality and reducing the impact of imperfection.
• We present three modules: ICEM identifying consis-
tency between test and training data, CDAM evaluating
data discrepancy across modalities and DFM fusing
multi-modal data by employing discounting methodolo-
gies. DFM also customizes the impact of each modality
based on data quality at a pixel level.
• We validate the proposed method on two distinct datasets,
BRATS2021 and an in-house pancreas dataset, compar-
ing it with both classic and uncertainty-based methods.
Our proposed framework performs well in both normal
scenarios and imperfection scenarios.
II. R ELATED WORKS
A. Multi-Modal Medical Image Segmentation
Many researchers have proposed multi-modal fusion meth-
ods to fully utilize the different information contained in
multi-modal data. The current multi-modal fusion methods can
be mainly divided into early fusion [7], [16], [17], interme-
diate fusion [18], [19], and decision fusion [20], [21]. Early
fusion methods mainly involve combining the raw data at the
level of the original data. The typical method is to simply
concatenate or add the data and then input it into a neural
network. Chang et al. [17] propose DPAFNet, based on dual-
path (DP) module and multi-scale attention fusion (MAF)
module. By concatenating multimodal inputs, the network
ensures precise tumor segmentation. Intermediate fusion is
widely used in multi-modal fusion methods, because it allows
for the combination of information from different modalities
in a more meaningful and interpretable way. For example,
Xu et al. [18] innovate a knowledge-guided multimodal fusion
methodology, which uses multi-phase self-attention module to
make full use of cross-modal information. Zhang et al. [19]
introduce a spatial aggregation module to encourages per-pixel
interactions between different phases. Decision fusion achieves
the final outcomes by integrating results from multiple phases
through methods, such as averaging. Guo et al. [20] employs
averaging to merge segmentation outputs from multimodal
CNNs to improve segmentation accuracy.
Although these methods offer high precision, they often rely
on empirical design to extract multi-phase information. Yet,
their results are not always explicitly interpreted, depriving
clinicians of effective insights into the models reliability in
uncertain scenarios.
B. Uncertainty-Based Medical Image Segmentation
Using uncertainty in segmentation helps identify regions
where the model’s predictions have a lower degree of
confidence. Uncertainty-based methods, as mentioned in [22],
can be divided into probabilistic-based, ensemble-based, and
evidence-based methods. Probabilistic-based [23], [24] meth-
ods capture ambiguity in the data by learning a distribution
over segmentations, rather than producing a single determin-
istic output. Through this technique, the model can provide
both the most likely segmentation result along with a measure
of uncertainty, indicating the level of confidence for each pixel.
Ensemble-based methods [12], [25] aim to quantify predictive
uncertainty in deep learning models. By training multiple
neural networks independently from different initializations,
this method constructs an ensemble of models. Evidence-based
methods [7], [26] use an evidential layer which can quantify
the evidence-based uncertainty using subject logic (SL) [13]
and Dempster-Shafer theory (DST) [27], [28]. Zou et al. [7]
propose a segmentation network which can generate robust
segmentation results and reliable uncertainty using subject
logic. Huang et al. [29] introduce an Evidential Segmentation
(ES) module that not only achieves improved segmentation
accuracy in 3D PET/CT imaging but also generates uncertainty
maps that effectively quantify classification uncertainty.
Although these methods have made progress in quantify
uncertainty, they fall short in resisting noise. They can effec-
tively capture areas of uncertainty when data corruption is
minimal, but fail to accurately measure uncertainty and yield
good segmentation results when the data is completely com-
promised.
III. M ETHODOLOGY
The overall framework of REDNet is shown in Fig.1. It is
composed of evidential-based uncertainty estimation mod-
ule, Intra-modality Consistency Evaluation Module (ICEM),
Cross-modality Difference Aggregation Module (CDAM), and
Discounting Fusion Module (DFM). We are initially provided
with a set of multi-modality data, denoted as X = {x i }Mi=1,
where M represents the total number of modalities, each
x i ∈ RD,H,W represents an original input from a specific
modality, X is the set of all modalities involved and D, H, W
is the size of the image. The proposed framework processes 3D
medical images, and all modules operate on volumetric data
to preserve 3D contextual information. For each individual
modality, an evidence representation ei is then computed
through a Subjective Logic Network:
ei = F i (x i ), (1)
where ei ∈ RC,D,H,W and C is the class number. Each

Next, the data is introduced to the Discounting Fusion Mod-
ule. Using the information received from ICEM and CDAM,

leading to a discount on the evidence ei acquired in Eq. (1).
The final process constitutes using the Dempster-Shafer (DS)
Evidence Theory for an integrated fusion, resulting in a final

B. Intra-Modality Consistency Evaluation Module

feature representation to ensure robust against imperfection.

C. Cross-Modality Difference Aggregator Module
To fully exploit the information between multimodal data,
we further propose a cross-modality diversity aggregator mod-
ule. When significant discrepancies are detected between a
specific modality and others, it suggests potential unreliability
in that modality (e.g., due to noise, artifacts, or modality-
specific biases). To mitigate this, the module adaptively
reduces the weight assigned to the unreliable modality in
the final prediction. This ensures that regions with incon-
sistent or noisy signals contribute less to the segmentation
outcome, thereby enhancing overall robustness. This module
integrates information from different modalities to enhance
system robustness and precision. It reduces the impact of
areas with significant discrepancies where different modalities
provide different information. This allows the model to focus
more on different information across modalities and minimizes
imperfection interference.

γ = max (e j , c),

D. Discounting Fusion Module

Trust discounting is a technique that scales beliefs accord-
ing to the assessed reliability of the information source.
By weighting the information in this way, we can achieve
a more detailed evaluation that considers both the content of
the evidence and the credibility of the information source.
Building upon discounting operator, we integrate the di n and
dc matrices, indicative of intra-modality and cross-modality
information, respectively, to calculate the discount factor. This
integration allows for a more granular calibration of the
discounting:
dk = (α ∗ di n) + (β ∗ dc)(α + β) , (13)
where α and β are hyperparameters, both of them are set
to the value of 1. This adjustment, taking into account both
intra-modality and cross-modality information, enables the
dynamic tuning of evidence based on the quality of the
modality before advancing to the fusion stage. By refining
the degree of uncertainty, it allows useful information to
play a more significant role while reducing the impact of
imperfection data. The discounting strategy is adaptive to data
quality: for high-quality inputs with minimal imperfections,
the computed discount factor d approaches 1, effectively
preserving the original segmentation. This ensures that the
framework defaults to standard predict when data reliability
is assured, avoiding unnecessary modifications.

IV. E XPERIMENT
A. Experimental Setup
1) Dataset: We evaluated REDNet on both external dataset
and in-house pancreas dataset. The external dataset con-
sists of 1251 MRI cases can be openly obtained from
the Multimodal Brain Tumor Segmentation Challenge 2021
(BraTS2021) [15]. The BraTS image segmentation challenge
started in 2012 and has been conducted yearly as a crucial
component of the MICCAI [32]. The BraTS dataset is a widely
used benchmark for brain tumor segmentation research. All the
imaging datasets have been segmented manually, by one to
four raters, following the same annotation protocol, and their
annotations were approved by experienced neuro-radiologists.
For each scan, there are four modalities: T1-weighted (T1),
post-contrast T1-weighted (T1Gd), T2-weighted(T2), and
T2 Fluid Attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR). Annota-
tions of the 1251 scans include the GD-enhancing tumor
(ET-label 4), the peritumoral edema (ED-label2), and the

Following [33], we divided the 1251 scans into 834, 208 and

Using the same pre-processing operation as in [33]. The
in-house dataset from Changhai Hospital includes 139 patients
diagnosed with either SCN (Serous Cystic Neoplasm) or MCN
(Mucinous Cystic Neoplasm). All volumes contain arterial
phases (AP), portal venous phases (VP), and delayed phases
(DP). Experienced radiologists annotated the pancreas and
tumor regions in the volumes. The in-plane size of volumes is
512 × 512 with spacing ranges from 0.546 mm to 0.896 mm,
and the number of slices ranges from 102 to 289. The
volumes of three phases are co-registered into venous phase
by Elastix [34] toolbox.
2) Implementation Details: The framework was implemented
in Python with the PyTorch-based medical image framework
MONAI and was trained and tested on a NVIDIA 4090 GPU.
We set the learning rate to 1e − 4 and the number of
epochs for model training to 200. Adopting the approach
from [40], we first trained our model on single modality
datasets using the trusted segmentation module to establish
a robust baseline for each modality independently. After this
initial stage, we engaged in advanced multi-modality train-
ing, combining the strengths of each individual modality to
enhance the model’s performance and accuracy. In training
stage, we initially identify the volume’s minimal bounding
box and then proceed to randomly split it into a volume size
of 128 × 128 × 128. The data augmentation techniques are
similar to [33]. In the test phase, we use the sliding window
method with an overlap rate of 0.6. In our experiments, we use
Dice score and 95% Hausdorff distance (HD95) to evaluate the
segmentation results.
B. Comparisons With Other Methods
Our work presents a comparative analysis of the pro-
posed REDNet model against well-established models. These
include CNN architectures such as Attention U-Net [35], 3D
U-Net [37], UNet++ [38], and transformer-based models
like UNETR [36], as well as a hybrid model [33] that
integrates both CNN and transformer techniques. Assessments
also extend to various uncertainty-based models [7], [12], [39].
All the baseline models and our proposed model are trained
with the same dataset split. The selection of the model was
based on performance in the validation set. To be fair, all
reported results are the direct output of the model without any
post-processing.
1) Overall Evaluation: We carried out tests on both
BRATS2021 and our in-house pancreas dataset. As shown
in Table II, our segmentation strategy displayed outstanding
performance without imperfection, outperforming most cur-
rent technologies in fundamental metrics such as Dice and
HD95. In the BraTS dataset, while it slightly trails the brain
tumor-focused CKD method in some aspects, it outperforms
other methods. On the in-house dataset, our method exceeds
the performance of other models. Our in-house pancreas
dataset includes real clinical data collected over 10+ years
from different scanners, which better reflect actual clinical
scenarios. Here, our method outperforms others because it is
designed to handle imperfections.
2) Evaluation on Model Reliable With Imperfection: To assess
the robustness of our proposed model against imperfection
interference, we conducted experiments simulating a range of
imperfect environments. Gaussian noise is a widely adopted
synthetic imperfection for evaluating robustness in both gen-
eral image processing and multi-modal frameworks. While
real-world multi-modal data may exhibit diverse imperfections
(e.g., motion artifacts, or modality-specific distortions). Gaus-
sian noise serving as a standardized benchmark is widely used
in research. Following [41], [42], and [43], we adopted the
addition of Gaussian noise to the input data. The noise model
is expressed mathematically as:
xnoi sy = x + N (0, σ2), (19)
where x represents the clean input data, while xnoi sy denotes
the corresponding data corrupted by additive noise. N (0, σ2)
is the Gaussian noise generator with a mean of zero and a
variance of σ 2.
As show in Fig. 2, the experiments are conducted on
two datasets and each represented by two rows of images.
Each dataset shows four different imperfection scenarios,
each depicted in a respective graph for both Dice and
HD95 metrics. Under noise-free conditions, our method might
not outperform the CKD-TransBTS method, which employs

Noise: Noise in MRI images follows a Rayleigh distribution,
particularly in low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) regions [44].

INU (also known as bias field) is a highly prevalent artifact in

inhomogeneities, causing the same tissue type to exhibit differ-

factors like magnetic field or radio frequency (RF) inhomo-
geneity and patient anatomy [47]. We applied synthetic INU
fields to the BraTS dataset to model this imperfection. We con-
ducted experiments on the BraTS dataset under Rayleigh noise
(scale=2) and INU conditions (magnitude=50). Our method
was compared against eight well-performed models. Our
method maintained high segmentation accuracy under both

3) Discussion: The proposed method is designed to address
general data imperfections by dynamically discounting unre-
liable modalities, rather than explicitly learning specific
imperfection patterns. This method enables generalization to
unseen imperfections, as it prioritizes modalities with higher
agreement and suppresses those exhibiting deviations from
the normal. Therefore, it demonstrates more robust perfor-
mance when facing practical problems. While our discounting
fusion module effectively suppresses unreliable modalities,
the discounting operator scales down belief masses even for
perfectly reliable data. Though the discount factor is close
to 1, it still reduces the belief values. This always-on discount-
ing slightly diminishes usable information from high-quality
sources. We hope to explore more reasonable discounting
mechanisms in future work.
V. C ONCLUSION
In summary, the proposed REDNet exhibits robustness by
addressing the issue of imperfection in multimodal medi-
cal image segmentation. Its reliable performance on both
the BRATS2021 dataset and in-house datasets underscores
its potential for clinical applications. With its combina-
tion of Intra-modality Consistency Evaluation Module and
Cross-Modality Difference Aggregator Module and Dis-
counting Fusion Module, REDNet dynamically adjusts the
contributions of different modalities, enhancing the reliability
in segmentation tasks.
Even when faced with challenging imperfection conditions,
REDNet consistently outperforms traditional segmentation
methods. Its ability to discern between reliable and imper-
fection data has significant implications for improving
computer-aided diagnosis systems, paving the way for
enhanced patient outcomes in clinical settings.
